description: Solo coder who likes space, maps, and turning messy data into something useful. Here to learn, build fast, and have fun with NASA data.
summary: BRASA is a web app that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections over Argentina into one consistent burning activity calendar. Satellites have tracked active fires since 2000, but the record is split between MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012). VIIRS sees many more small fires, so simply combining the two makes fire activity look like it doubled in 2012, and again in 2018 when NOAA-20 joined. BRASA calibrates MODIS to VIIRS on the 14 years both sensors flew, removing those fake jumps; tested year by year, the harmonized record predicts what VIIRS actually saw with r = 0.985 and 3.5% average annual error for Argentina as a whole. Responders, scientists and land managers can pick any area, see its monthly burning calendar from 2000 to 2025, spot extreme months and the fire season, see whether cropland, forest or grassland is burning, compare this week's live NASA detections with 25 years of history, and see whether this year is heading for a record. A consistent record matters because you can only call a fire season unusual if you can compare it fairly with the past.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

BRASA (Spanish for "ember") is a burning activity calendar for Argentina built on 5.67 million NASA fire detections from 2000 to 2025. On one page, a user can:

- Pick an area (Paraná Delta, Córdoba Sierras, Gran Chaco, Andean Patagonia, all of Argentina) or draw their own box on the map

- Switch between "Old satellite only" (MODIS), "Both mixed (wrong)" and "BRASA blended" to see the fake 2012 and 2018 jumps appear and disappear

- Read a plain-English sentence for any area and month, such as "July 2020 was the worst July in 25 years in Paraná Delta"

- Play the hexagon map through 25 years, in 2D or 3D

- See a month-by-year calendar of burning, with extreme months outlined automatically

- See the fire season for that area (when it starts, peaks and ends) and whether it is shifting

- See what is burning: cropland, forest and woodland, or grass, shrub and wetland

- Compare the last 5 days of live NASA detections with 25 years of history for the same month

- See whether this year is heading for a record, with a projection for the full year

- Use the app in English or Spanish, share any view as a link, and download an area's monthly data as a CSV

- Take a 60-second guided tour of real events, such as the 2020 and 2008 Paraná Delta fires

HOW IT WORKS

1. Clean: vegetation fires only; MODIS confidence 30 or higher; VIIRS nominal or high confidence. Volcanoes, gas flares and offshore sources are removed.

2. Grid: every detection goes into an equal-area H3 hexagon (about 252 km²). Activity is counted as fire-active hexagon-days, which removes most of the 1 km vs 375 m pixel-size difference.

3. Calibrate: on 2012–2025, when both sensors flew, fit log(VIIRS) = a[month] + b · log(MODIS), with b = 0.88. Terra alone is calibrated separately before Aqua launched in 2002; NOAA-20 is calibrated to Suomi NPP to fill gaps.

4. Adjust locally and extend: each ~12,000 km² area learns a small correction from the overlap years. Before 2012, MODIS is scaled to VIIRS-equivalent values with a 90% uncertainty range.

5. Validate: each year from 2012 to 2025 is hidden, predicted from MODIS alone, and compared with what VIIRS saw. Result: r = 0.985 and 3.5% average yearly error for Argentina; Gran Chaco 3.9%, Córdoba 14%, Andean Patagonia 15%, Paraná Delta 24% (small areas are less certain, and the app says so). A model trained only on 2019–2025 predicts 2012–2014 with 2.0% error, so the calibration does not drift over time.

6. Classify: each detection is matched to NASA's MODIS land cover map (MCD12Q1) for its year.

7. Live: server functions pull NASA FIRMS near-real-time VIIRS NOAA-20 data, remove 154 known gas-flare and industrial hexagons, and compare this week and this year with the harmonized history.

BENEFITS

- Emergency responders see at a glance whether this week is normal, above normal or at record pace for their area.

- Scientists get one consistent 25-year record with tested calibration and uncertainty, instead of two records that cannot be compared.

- Land managers see when the fire season starts and peaks and whether burning is agricultural or wildland, so they can plan monitoring and prevention.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

We want fire records to be trusted across sensor changes. The method works for any country with NASA FIRMS data, and it is ready for the next sensor change: Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026, and the record now continues on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Next steps: extend to all of South America, add daily resolution, and add weather and drought layers to explain extreme seasons.

TOOLS

Data pipeline: Python with DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, h3 and rasterio. Web app: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, deck.gl, Apache ECharts, h3-js. Hosting: Vercel. Code: https://github.com/rinayp2009-alt/Brasa

USE OF AI AND MY CONTRIBUTIONS

I built BRASA as a solo high school participant, using Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, as a coding, writing and editing partner.

What I did:

- Chose the challenge and the project direction: a harmonized fire calendar for Argentina, built for responders, scientists and land managers

- Set up the data: created my NASA Earthdata, FIRMS and AppEEARS accounts, and downloaded and organized 26 years of FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS fire archives and 48 MODIS land cover files

- Set up the project infrastructure: the GitHub repository, Vercel hosting and the secure NASA FIRMS API key behind the live data

- Made the design and feature decisions: the satellite toggle that shows the fake 2012 jump, the live "Right now" panel, the 3D map, the Spanish version, the record tracker and the guided tour

- Tested the app as a user, found bugs (such as wrong colors on the first switch to 3D) and directed the fixes

- Reviewed the results, and chose to show uncertainty honestly where the data is weaker

- Planned the demo video, chose the final version and published the submission

How AI was used:

- Claude helped write the Python data pipeline, the React web app and the serverless live-data functions.

- Claude helped assemble the demo video from frame-by-frame captures of the real BRASA website, with title cards and a soundtrack synthesized in code. There are no AI-generated images, voices or footage, and the end card says the video was edited with AI assistance.

All data comes from NASA and is processed by code in the public GitHub repository, so every result can be reproduced.
